subject.title: Confessions
subject.author: Robert Browning
subject.text:
What is he buzzing in my ears?
"Now that I come to die,
Do I view the world as a vale of tears?"
Ah, reverend sir, not I!

What I viewed there once, what I view again
Where the physic bottles stand
On the table's edge,-is a suburb lane,
With a wall to my bedside hand.

That lane sloped, much as the bottles do,
From a house you could descry
O'er the garden-wall; is the curtain blue
Or green to a healthy eye?

To mine, it serves for the old June weather
Blue above lane and wall;
And that farthest bottle labelled "Ether"
Is the house o'ertopping all.

At a terrace, somewhere near the stopper,
There watched for me, one June,
A girl: I know, sir, it's improper,
My poor mind's out of tune.

Only, there was a way... you crept
Close by the side, to dodge
Eyes in the house, two eyes except:
They styled their house "The Lodge."

What right had a lounger up their lane?
But, by creeping very close,
With the good wall's help,-their eyes might strain
And stretch themselves to Oes,

Yet never catch her and me together,
As she left the attic, there,
By the rim of the bottle labelled "Ether,"
And stole from stair to stair,

And stood by the rose-wreathed gate. Alas,
We loved, sir-used to meet:
How sad and bad and mad it was-
But then, how it was sweet!

title: The One Scene in the Book Browning Wasn't Arguing About
standfirst: Dramatis Personae is a book full of Robert Browning picking fights — with doubters, with mediums, with his own grief. In the middle of it, a dying stranger remembers a love affair that broke exactly the rule Browning had broken himself, and isn't sorry for a second of it.

sections.heading: A Clergyman Asks for Remorse. He Isn't Granted Any.
sections.body:
The question comes secondhand, the way it always does at a deathbed: a clergyman leaning in, asking whether, now that it has come to this, the dying man sees the whole business — life, the world, the lot of it — as a vale of tears.

> "Now that I come to die,
> Do I view the world as a vale of tears?"
>
> Ah, reverend sir, not I!

That is the entire exchange Robert Browning allows before the real poem starts. "Confessions" is a dramatic monologue first published in his 1864 collection Dramatis Personae, and it spends its nine stanzas refusing the script a bedside scene is supposed to follow. No contrition, no inventory of sins. What the old man wants to talk about instead is a girl, a wall, and a row of medicine bottles.

sections.heading: Nine Bottles Become a Street
sections.body:
What keeps the poem from sounding merely contrary is the mechanism Browning builds to get there. Lying in bed, the dying man looks at the "physic bottles" lined up on his table and sees, instead, the suburb lane outside a house he loved decades earlier: the lane "sloped, much as the bottles do," and the tallest bottle on the table, the one "labelled 'Ether,'" stands for the house "o'ertopping all" the rest of the street. It is a small, exact piece of engineering — a sickroom rebuilt, object by object, into a place forty years gone.

The form plays a related trick. Each stanza alternates a four-beat line with a three-beat one, the metre of a ballad or a hymn — a pattern one close reading [calls bouncy and singsong](https://litcharts.com/poetry/robert-browning/confessions). That is the cadence of devotional verse, borrowed here for a man who has just told his minister he feels no remorse at all. The tune doesn't fit the scene. That mismatch is the joke, and the point.

sections.heading: The Girl at the House They Called The Lodge
sections.body:
The romance itself is sketched in a handful of details and nothing more, which is very much in keeping with the form — a dramatic monologue only knows what the situation would actually produce. There was a terrace, a particular June, a girl who watched for him there. There was a wall he learned to creep along "to dodge / Eyes in the house, two eyes except" — her family's, or whoever ran that household — while he remembers, half-mocking even now, that they "styled their house 'The Lodge.'" Styled is doing real work in that line: it's the word of a man who noticed, even while besotted, that the name was a touch grand for what it was.

One reading of the poem [takes her for a servant girl](https://davidsuttonpoetry.com/2016/08/12/week-198-confessions-by-robert-browning/) at that house, which would sharpen the transgression into something crossing a line Victorian households drew between a family and its staff. The poem itself never says so outright — it only gives us eyes to dodge, and a girl who "stole from stair to stair" to reach the attic and the "rose-wreathed gate" where they actually met.

sections.heading: The Calm Corner in an Argumentative Book
sections.body:
"Confessions" appeared in Dramatis Personae, Browning's first new collection in nine years — his first since Men and Women in 1855. It arrived out of a particular silence. He and Elizabeth Barrett Browning had lived in Italy since their marriage; she died in Florence on 29 June 1861, and he returned to London with their son not long afterward. The book that followed is, by most accounts, a quarrelsome one, built from poems that argue with Victorian doubt, with spiritualism, with the fashionable biblical criticism of the day, voiced through everyone from a cheating medium to Shakespeare's Caliban.

"Confessions" sits apart from most of that. One academic survey of the collection [singles it out as one of its finest poems](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/literature-and-writing/dramatis-personae-robert-browning), precisely because it isn't fighting anything — no theology to defend, no sceptic to answer, just an old man and a memory. It doesn't need the rest of the book's argument to work, which may be exactly why it has outlasted some of the poems that do.

sections.heading: A Franker Elegy, Written a Few Pages Earlier
sections.body:
The same book contains "Prospice," a much more direct piece of writing: Browning speaking in his own voice, not through an invented old man, about facing death and expecting to find Elizabeth Barrett Browning again on the other side of it. It was written in the autumn of 1861, within months of her death.

Set the two poems side by side and Dramatis Personae starts to look like a book working through the same loss twice, in two different registers. "Prospice" takes death head-on and answers it with doctrine — a soul, a reunion, a fight worth having. "Confessions" comes at death from an angle, through a stranger's voice and a stranger's romance, and answers it with nothing more doctrinal than a memory that still feels sweet. Browning seems to have needed both: the poem that argues for an afterlife, and the one that only remembers being alive.

sections.heading: The Same Risk He Had Taken Himself, Twenty Years Before
sections.body:
It is hard to read the old man's lack of remorse as entirely a stranger's once you know what Browning had already done with his own life. He had fallen for Elizabeth Barrett through letters, against the wishes of her father, Edward Moulton-Barrett, who viewed him as "an unreliable fortune hunter" and who, by his own daughter's account, "disinherited her, as he did each one of his children who got married without his permission" — permission he never gave to any of them. On 12 September 1846, while her family was away, Elizabeth left the house to marry Browning at St Marylebone Parish Church, went home for a week to hide what she had done, and then left for Italy with her husband. She never saw her father again, and he never forgave her.

Fifteen years later she died in Florence — "in her husband's arms," by one account of her life — and three years after that, Browning handed a dying stranger his own unfinished argument with respectability, and let him win it without a flicker of guilt. "How sad and bad and mad it was— / But then, how it was sweet!" is not a line Browning needed to invent. He had already lived a version of it.
